summary: Aubergine, sweet potato, pepper and chickpeas roasted under harissa, with slices of halloumi laid on for the last stretch and a garlic yoghurt stirred together while it bakes. The hearty vegetarian main of this set: the tin of chickpeas carries it, and nothing needs timing to the minute.

ingredients.note: Milk. The source cuts it into 8 slices.
Heat and ingredients vary widely between brands; read the jar.

ingredients.quantity: The source scatters it to finish and gives no weight.
The source seasons the dressing to taste and gives no weight.

method.instruction: Heat the oven to 200°C conventional, or 180°C fan (gas mark 6). Both figures are stated by the source; neither is a conversion made here. Line a baking tray with baking paper unless it is non-stick.

Cut the aubergine and sweet potato into rounds half an inch thick — about 1.3 cm, converted here by arithmetic rather than stated by the source — then quarter the rounds. Cut the pepper into large chunks.
Put the vegetables and the drained chickpeas in a bowl, add the tablespoon of oil and the harissa, and mix until everything is coated.
Tip onto the tray in a single layer and bake for 30 minutes.

Cut the halloumi into 8 slices, lay them over the vegetables and return the tray for a further 10 to 15 minutes, until the vegetables are cooked through — a knife should meet no resistance in the sweet potato.
Stir the yoghurt, garlic, teaspoon of oil, salt and pepper together, spoon over the finished tray and scatter with parsley.

yield_note: Serves 4, as stated by the source. Source times: 5 minutes preparation and 40 minutes cooking, 45 minutes in total. The source gives no resting time, and none is invented here.

provenance_note: Recipe facts paraphrased from Sarah Howells' page at The Gluten Free Blogger, accessed 2026-09-14. Two notes on what is and is not claimed here. The source gives its piece size in inches; the centimetre figure above is plain arithmetic and is labelled as such. The source publishes in a gluten-free context, but this record makes no gluten-free claim: harissa pastes and halloumi brands differ, and only the packet in your hand can answer that. The source writes tablespoons and teaspoons without stating a millilitre value, so no spoon size is asserted here.

caveats: No meat, poultry or fish is involved, so no internal-temperature threshold applies. The endpoint is texture: the sweet potato should take a knife without resistance.
Allergens: milk, in both the halloumi and the yoghurt. Harissa recipes vary between brands and some contain additional allergens.
Halloumi is a brined cheese and already salty; the source adds no salt to the tray itself.
